submissions.findingTextShort: A randomized multiple-ascending-dose phase-I study established short-term oral baicalein exposure and tolerability, not efficacy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled multiple-ascending-dose phase-I study, 36 healthy adults received oral baicalein tablet regimens at 200, 400, or 600 mg with repeated dosing; the study characterized pharmacokinetics and short-term tolerability and cannot support influenza, Parkinson disease, cognition, inflammatory-disease, or anticancer efficacy.
submissions.usageContext: Oral baicalein tablets in multiple-ascending-dose phase-I regimens
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Short-duration healthy-volunteer PK/safety evidence only; target-patient efficacy and long-term safety remain unresolved.

submissions.findingTextShort: Single-dose baicalein was studied from 100 to 2800 mg in 72 healthy adults with only mild treatment-related adverse events.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized double-blind phase-I trial administered single oral baicalein doses from 100 to 2800 mg to 72 healthy adults, documenting pharmacokinetics and eleven treatment-related adverse events that were all mild and resolved without further treatment; this supports short-term exposure characterization but not therapeutic benefit or broad consumer-dose selection.
submissions.usageContext: Single oral baicalein doses from 100 to 2800 mg
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Healthy-volunteer, single-dose setting; absence of serious short-term events does not establish long-term or disease-population safety.

submissions.findingTextShort: Human phase-I baicalein evidence raises evidence freshness but must remain below an efficacy ceiling.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The direct human baicalein literature currently establishes oral exposure, pharmacokinetics, food effects, and short-term tolerability in healthy volunteers; these phase-I data should replace a purely preclinical evidence description but must not be promoted into efficacy claims for disease or wellness outcomes without direct later-phase human trials.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Research-gap conclusion; human exposure does not equal demonstrated clinical efficacy.

submissions.findingTextShort: Human trans-anethole metabolism was characterized at a 1 mg dose close to dietary exposure.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A human radiolabel metabolism study administered trans-anethole at a 1 mg dose described as close to dietary exposure and characterized urinary and expired-air disposition; this establishes food-level human metabolism but does not support digestive or anti-inflammatory efficacy or the safety of concentrated essential-oil or supplement exposures.
submissions.populationContext: Human volunteers in a radiolabeled food-flavor metabolism study
submissions.usageContext: Purified trans-anethole 1 mg, near dietary flavor exposure
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Low-dose pharmacokinetic/metabolic evidence only; concentrated exposures require separate safety and intervention evidence.

submissions.findingTextShort: Anethole evidence must separate trans- from cis-anethole and purified dietary exposure from fennel or anise essential oils.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The anethole evidence graph must distinguish trans-anethole from cis-anethole, purified molecule exposure from fennel, anise, or star-anise essential oils, and food-level flavor exposure from concentrated supplement or oil exposure; botanical or essential-oil outcomes and toxicity cannot be assigned to isolated trans-anethole without composition-compatible receipts.
submissions.populationContext: Human and product evidence involving anethole-containing exposures
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Identity rule; does not assert concentrated trans-anethole is safe or unsafe without dedicated evidence.
